title: Most AI Detectors Fail Silently. We Built One That Prints Its Limits on the Label.
partialText:
Panoptes (https://github.com/marketstandard/Panoptes) is an open-source, local-first workbench for AI-text attribution. It reports calibrated probabilities instead of binary verdicts, tests watermarks with measurable power limits, and makes every artifact hash-signed and reproducible.

A university IT department pastes a student essay into a free “AI detector.” The tool returns 98% AI-generated. The essay was written in 2019.

If you’ve followed AI-text detection at all, you’ve probably seen some version of this story. A model trained to separate “human” from “machine” text on one distribution gets pointed at a slightly different one, such as a new model family, a paraphrased passage, or a non-native English writer. The confidence doesn’t drop because the architecture has no mechanism for recognizing that shift.

We spent the last cycle building Panoptes, an open-source evidence workbench designed around a different question. Instead of stopping at “AI or not?”, it asks: “What does the evidence actually support for this kind of text, given what we calibrated on, and when should the system abstain?”

What follows covers the design rules, the numbers, the watermark forensics, and the things we’re explicitly not claiming.

Rule one: a detector score is not a probability

Most tools ship a raw classifier score dressed up as a probability. Panoptes treats that score as a feature and makes the statistical steps explicit:

  1. Raw scores pass through an isotonic-regression map fitted on a verified reference corpus. Every report includes the calibration bundle ID, cohort, prevalence, and reliability error.
  2. The calibrated probability becomes a likelihood ratio and is combined with a user-declared prior. If you tell the system you expect 5% AI text in the population, the posterior respects that. The same document can and should land differently in different populations.
  3. Expected calibration error is reported as a diagnostic of the map. It is never silently folded into the posterior.

The UI exposes all of this, including posterior decomposition, Wilson intervals, FDR-adjusted q-values, and reliability diagrams. Those details live in a “technical laboratory” one disclosure layer below the plain-language answer.

Rule two: separate the evidence channels

Panoptes keeps different types of attribution evidence separate by construction so they do not contaminate one another:

  • Passive AI participation: stylometric + neural estimates of machine involvement, including a contribution-fraction head for human-AI co-writing.
  • Watermark hypothesis tests: known public schemes (KGW green-list z-scores, Unicode zero-width), reported as p-values with per-token overlays. A p-value is not “the probability of a watermark,” and a negative result is not evidence of human authorship. The UI says so every time.
  • Source-family similarity: open-set attribution across calibrated model families with an explicit unknown state. The system can say “this resembles nothing we’ve calibrated” instead of forcing a guess.
  • Cryptographic provenance: C2PA manifest verification for uploads that carry signed provenance.

Each channel produces its own evidence. A Bayesian layer combines them only at the end.

How well does it transfer?

In-domain accuracy is not enough. In production, the harder problem is whether a detector holds up on text from new populations. We made that the main evaluation: leave-one-dataset-out across MAGE, RAID, and DeFactify, with calibration-transfer matrices.

The frozen three-seed neural ensemble has a mean held-out AUROC of 0.802, compared with 0.64 to 0.69 for every classical tier. Its worst held-out cohort, at 0.658, still sits above every classical tier’s mean. In these results, calibration transfers better than representation: the calibrator’s off-diagonal Brier score degrades only 0.024 → 0.028 under transfer.

There is also a negative result worth calling out. On real CoAuthor co-writing sessions, where documents are ~21% machine-written, the ranking inverts. The neural ensemble is the most conservative tier, which makes sense because a 21%-machine document is not the binary positive anyone trained for. The contribution-fraction head stays external-evaluation-only until a terms-cleared mixed-authorship cohort exists. We state that constraint explicitly in the paper.

Watermark forensics: three questions nobody was measuring

Provider watermarks in the SynthID-Text family are shipping in production models now. v2.1 adds three signed evaluation cards that treat watermarking as a measurement problem:

1. Does sampling temperature decide whether a watermark exists at all? We swept temperature from 0.0 to 1.3 against matched watermark-strength generations. Detection power collapses as temperature drops. At greedy decoding (T=0), there is a true dead zone: with no sampling randomness left to steer, the scheme has nothing to embed into. If you assume watermarks survive API temperature settings, that assumption needs to be measured first:

python -m bench.run_watermark_temperature   # signed card: cards/watermark-temperature.json

2. Do watermarks survive distillation? Yes, and we can measure it. Student models trained on watermarked teacher outputs inherit a detectable green-list bias (“radioactivity”), and the card quantifies the trade-off: paraphrase-pre and negative-delta neutralization arms against knowledge preservation.

python -m bench.run_radioactivity           # signed card: cards/radioactivity.json

3. What happens when watermarked text leaks into your calibration corpus? For contamination governance, baseline manifests carry a declared watermark status. Anthropic runs past the EU-transition date default to suspected. The corpus summary aggregates per-cohort status, and a public-scheme smoke screen audits the human controls. When a flagged cohort is loaded for calibration, the live analyzer appends a limitation to the report. We treat watermarks as a calibration confound and as lineage evidence, not as courtroom proof of distillation.

Signed and reproducible artifacts

Every figure in the UI renders from a hash-signed JSON artifact. Corpus records verify against SHA-256 manifests with Merkle roots. Third-party datasets ship as pointer manifests containing hashes and counts, never raw text. The reproduction path from a clean checkout is documented and self-checking:

git clone https://github.com/marketstandard/Panoptes.git
cd Panoptes
python -m venv .venv && .venv\Scripts\activate   # Windows
pip install -e backend[dev]
cd frontend && npm install && npm run build && cd ..
panoptes up --profile local-gpu                  # or: --profile fixture

Panoptes also has a runtime plugin loader (PANOPTES_PLUGIN_PATHS) so operators can add their own watermark or detector adapters. Plugins are namespaced plugin:<id> and wrapped so a misbehaving plugin degrades to an abstention instead of crashing an analysis.

What we’re not claiming

  • Private vendor watermark keys remain undetectable to us. We characterize the public-scheme family, not Anthropic’s production key.
  • Radioactivity shows training lineage, not intent or authorization.
  • The human reference cohort is small (n=104 records). Hypothesis tests are underpowered for small effects, and the paper says so with numbers.
  • No output of this system is proof of authorship. It is calibrated evidence with stated transport limits, which is the most any system like this should claim.

Read the paper, break the system

The full paper has 33 references, all the math, and every caveat. It is free to read:

  • Paper: https://marketstandard.github.io/Panoptes/paper.html
  • Code: https://github.com/marketstandard/Panoptes
  • Frozen neural weights: https://huggingface.co/MarketStandard/panoptes-neural-v1

Reproductions, adversarial reviews, and external-detector harness runs (python -m bench evaluate-repo <url>) are genuinely welcome. The point of shipping signed artifacts is that you can check our work instead of trusting it.

Panoptes is built by Carrington Junior and Trey Huffine. If this was useful, a star on the repo helps. A skeptical issue helps more.

Most AI Detectors Fail Silently. We Built One That Prints Its Limits on the Label. was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
